explanation: Fires on concrete physical or sensory descriptive nouns and adjectives, especially body parts and textures (eyebrows/brow, fingers, breasts, crunchy, spherical, rubber, velcro, garlic, glued). Top is 'eyebrows' at 100%; other tactile or material words reach about 35-75%. Function words and code tokens give only weak activation.

Fires on honorific titles before a surname, above all 'Mr' or the period after 'Mr.'/'Ms.' (strong, 75-100%), and also 'miss'. Other titles (Dr, Capt, Secretary, Prof, Lord, Baron) give moderate to weak activation.

Fires strongly on many common function words and generic words, especially 'or' in lists, prepositions completing a verb ('think of', 'deal with'), and 'more', 'known', 'items', 'thing'. These are mostly in the middle of question or descriptive prose. There is no clear content-specific trigger.

Fires on spatial position or side words describing parts of objects or places: opposite, upper/lower, outer/inner, surface, corner(s), side, south/southern, front, bottom, ventral, circumferentially. It is strongest in patent or technical descriptions of physical structure. Other words are weak.

Fires on digits inside identifier numbers such as legal docket or case numbers (No. PD-1240, 02-CR-134), statute and standard numbers, DOI or reference IDs, and route numbers. It is strongest on an early or middle digit of the code. Ordinary quantities, dates and decimals are weak.

Fires on word-internal subword fragments containing 'l' or 'yl'/'il'/'el' clusters, especially in chemical names (sialyl, silyl, myel, diacylglycerol, polysilicon) and similar letter sequences in names (Sylveon, Siegel, Hyllas, Seville). It responds to the spelling fragment, not the meaning.

Fires on a token that completes a fixed phrase or a head+preposition construction in formal or academic or legal text. Examples are court-name words (Court of Criminal Appeals, Superior Court, Judge), and prepositions after a head noun or participle (parents of, families with, filed against, licensed to, sample of). The token is predictable from the preceding words.

Fires on the digits inside academic citation markers such as [@pone.0152851.ref001], [@CR4], [@B3], [@b13]. It is strongest on the final reference-number digit. Brackets, '@' and the punctuation of citation lists get moderate activation, and other parenthetical citations are weak.

Mostly fires on 'or' in paired alternatives or comparisons ('superior or comparable', 'little or no', 'with or without', 'rarely or never'). It also fires on digits inside numbers, timestamps and version strings, and on some name tokens. These are several loosely connected triggers.

Heterogeneous: fires on the period or newline closing a judge or court line in legal citations, on digits in chemical names or citation IDs, on code tokens (event names, @subpackage), and on various mid-phrase content words. No common feature is evident.

Fires on mid-word subword fragments in technical compounds, such as runs of zeros, 'ocyte' (adipocyte, leukocyte), 'ovolta', 'renal' (adrenaline), 'ro' (nitro), '-Version' in MIME-Version, and '\Framework'. These are mostly scientific word-piece completions plus some code and header tokens.

Fires on bracketing and operator tokens inside nested math expressions and code: closing or opening parens and braces, '(\' and '}\' in LaTeX, '>()', '[[' or '],', and digits or variables inside parenthesized formulas. It is strongest deep within nested brackets.

Fires strongly on the colon after a parameter name in a typed function signature (Swift/Kotlin/TypeScript 'name: Type'). It fires moderately on other key: value or label colons and citation colons ('65:3160'). It is weak on assorted word fragments.

Fires on tokens in the import or include header at the top of a source file: '.h' or '.hh' in #include lines, 'import', 'use', 'const' or 'require' lines, 'std' after 'using namespace', and module path parts (type_traits, .helpers). It is strongest just before or within a dependency declaration.

Fires on hopeful or helpful aspirational language in first-person or promotional prose: 'hopefully', 'hope', 'cope', 'work hard to', 'find inspiration', 'make you feel at home', 'positive impact'. Other tokens like '#ifndef' after license headers are weaker oddities.

Fires on a word that continues a verb phrase in narrative or expository prose, often a preposition, auxiliary or verb after the subject or modal (put him at, can make it, not taking, after being charged, were enrolled, have). It also fires on 'LICENSE' in the standard BSD header line. This is broad syntactic continuation without a specific concept.

Fires on the first subword of a proper name split into pieces (Pe-zold, Pe-ugeot, Man-awatu, May-awati, Gh-ulam, AP-PELLATE). It also fires on assorted tokens in license boilerplate ('to use, copy') and chemical prefixes. This is mostly word-start fragments of multi-token names.

Fires on the first or early subword of a word split into fragments, mostly in non-English text (Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, German, Hungarian, CJK byte pieces), e.g. 'dif'undir, 'z'it, 'f'izesse. It also fires on some English fragments and license verbs ('use', 'under').

Fires on a subword fragment containing 'ad'/'ud'/'od'/'ed' (often 'd' plus a vowel) in the middle of a proper name or rare word: Hadley, Guadagnini, Prudential, Hodges, Pedro, cadaver, Hodgkin, Nadia. It is strongest when the fragment begins or continues a name; common words are weak.

Fires on religious or devotional Christian language: God is holy and 'pure', the Lord will 'call', God's 'Kingdom', 'called', 'justified', 'raised up by God'. It is strongest on the theological predicate word. Other contexts are weak and noisy.

Fires on the final piece of multi-token nouns or suffixes ('-ability' in tolerability/acceptability, 'groups' in subgroups) and on some standalone nouns (temple, lion, ritual, demon, shrinking). No single semantic theme is evident.
